analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 1992 cable law that forced cable companies to roll back their rates.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors, never left a House subcommittee, and died without a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1992, Congress passed a law restoring federal regulation of cable television after rates climbed following earlier deregulation, and the FCC began implementing it. This bill would have repealed that law, returning cable to its earlier, largely unregulated status, while keeping one piece (the rules on broadcasters' retransmission consent and satellite TV obligations) in place. It would also have wiped out the FCC regulations written to carry out the 1992 law. Despite a title suggesting consumer protection, its main effect would have been to free cable operators from the rate rollbacks and consumer rules the 1992 law imposed.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable television operators. Repealing the 1992 law would have lifted the FCC's authority over cable rates and voided the regulations the agency had issued under it, letting operators set rates as they wished. Broadcasters and satellite providers would have kept the retransmission-consent and satellite provisions the bill carved out.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Cable Television Consumer Protection and Competition Act of 1992, treating the sections of the Communications Act it amended as if they had never been changed, except for the retransmission-consent provisions.

Makes any FCC regulations prescribed to implement the 1992 Act cease to be effective on enactment, requiring the Commission to amend or rescind them, which would have eliminated the rate rules then taking effect.
Preserves section 25 of the 1992 Act, which the CRS summary identifies with retransmission consent and direct broadcast satellite obligations, so those rules would have continued unchanged.

analysis.who_pays: Cable subscribers, who would lose the federal rate protections the 1992 law restored — the very rates the FCC was in the process of rolling back — and would face higher bills with fewer avenues for recourse.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the 1992 Act would have removed the rate regulation it restored, allowing cable operators to raise rates on a service that by then reached most American homes.

The FCC's implementing regulations — including the rate rollbacks and customer-service standards issued under the 1992 Act — would have been voided on enactment, undoing protections subscribers had just gained.
The bill was narrowly drawn for one industry: it kept the retransmission-consent provisions broadcasters valued while stripping the provisions that constrained cable operators.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits run almost entirely to cable operators, who stood to escape rate rollbacks and consumer rules; the cost falls on subscribers through higher rates. The title, 'Cable Consumer Protection Act,' describes the opposite of the bill's main effect on the public. An honest case for it would rest on a belief that rate regulation distorts the market — but the bill offers nothing for consumers in exchange.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Telecommunications and Finance Subcommittee, where it sat with no cosponsors and no action until the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Barton of Texas introduced the bill on September 28, 1993, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On October 5, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 103rd Congress.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party.
Because it was never enacted, the 1992 cable law and the FCC regulations issued under it remained in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable subscribers are better off that the bill failed: the rate rollbacks and consumer protections restored by the 1992 law stayed on the books, and cable operators gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cable subscribers, who kept their rate protections

for.name: Rep. Joe Barton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the 1992 cable law; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in the 103rd Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Telecommunications and Finance Subcommittee, where it received no markup, no vote, and no further action for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the record shows one Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and a Democratic-run committee that never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have repealed the 1992 law that restored FCC authority over cable rates and would have voided the FCC's implementing regulations, freeing operators to raise rates on subscribers. The industry's gain would have come directly out of household cable bills.
